title: The Letter That Took a Year
learning_objectives: Read a chapter-length story with two timelines
Infer why a character delays, using scattered clues
Distinguish what a character says from what they mean
parent_prompts: Let the child read alone; it is long. After: why did Nia keep not sending the letter? The story never says outright. What finally made her send it?

pages.text: The letter began in January, on the first day of the new school year's second term, when Nia's best friend Hoa moved away. Not far, as grown-ups measure things: three hours on the bus, to a town by the coast where Hoa's mother had a new job. But three hours on a bus might as well be the moon when you are ten and nobody will drive you. "Write to me," Hoa said from the bus window. "Real letters. On paper." "Every week," said Nia. The bus pulled out. Nia went home and started the first letter that afternoon. She did not send it. This is the story of why.
pages.illustration_brief: A bus pulling away; Hoa's face at the window; Nia (purple overalls) on the pavement, one hand half-raised.
pages.audio_script: The letter began in January, on the first day of the new school year's second term, when Nia's best friend Hoa moved away. Not far, as grown-ups measure things: three hours on the bus, to a town by the coast where Hoa's mother had a new job. But three hours on a bus might as well be the moon when you are ten and nobody will drive you. Write to me, Hoa said from the bus window. Real letters. On paper. Every week, said Nia. The bus pulled out. Nia went home and started the first letter that afternoon. She did not send it. This is the story of why.
pages.image_alt: Nia waving as a bus with her friend Hoa drives off down the road.

pages.text: The first letter was two pages long and mostly about the bus stop. Nia read it over and thought it was boring. Hoa was by the sea now; she would have beaches and boats to write about, and Nia had a bus stop. She put the letter in her desk drawer and decided to wait until something interesting happened. In February something did: Nia won the class spelling prize. She started a new letter about that. Halfway down the page she thought, this sounds like boasting. Into the drawer it went, on top of the first.
pages.illustration_brief: A desk drawer open, two folded letters inside; a small spelling-prize ribbon on the desk.
pages.audio_script: The first letter was two pages long and mostly about the bus stop. Nia read it over and thought it was boring. Hoa was by the sea now; she would have beaches and boats to write about, and Nia had a bus stop. She put the letter in her desk drawer and decided to wait until something interesting happened. In February something did: Nia won the class spelling prize. She started a new letter about that. Halfway down the page she thought, this sounds like boasting. Into the drawer it went, on top of the first.
pages.image_alt: Nia at her desk reading over a two-page letter, an open drawer beside her.

pages.text: In March a letter arrived from Hoa. It was one page, written fast, full of crossings-out. The new school was fine. The sea was cold. She had a friend called Bich who was all right. "You have not written," it ended. "Are you cross?" Nia read it four times. Then she took out a fresh sheet and wrote NO, I AM NOT CROSS in capital letters, and stopped, because what came next? Sorry I have been boring? Sorry I won a prize? She folded the sheet round Hoa's letter and put them both in the drawer.
pages.illustration_brief: Nia at her desk holding a one-page letter with crossings-out; a fresh sheet with three capital-letter words.
pages.audio_script: In March a letter arrived from Hoa. It was one page, written fast, full of crossings-out. The new school was fine. The sea was cold. She had a friend called Bich who was all right. You have not written, it ended. Are you cross? Nia read it four times. Then she took out a fresh sheet and wrote NO, I AM NOT CROSS in capital letters, and stopped, because what came next? Sorry I have been boring? Sorry I won a prize? She folded the sheet round Hoa's letter and put them both in the drawer.
pages.image_alt: An envelope and a one-page letter full of crossings-out; the sea in a small picture.

pages.text: April, May, June. Each month Nia wrote something. Each month the drawer took it. The problem was no longer boring or boasting. The problem was the pile. Any letter she sent now would have to explain the pile, and every explanation she tried sounded worse than silence. "I have been busy" was a lie. "I did not know what to say" was true and sounded pathetic. The longer she waited, the bigger the first letter would have to be, and the bigger it had to be, the less she could write it.
pages.illustration_brief: The drawer now stuffed with folded letters; a calendar on the wall with months crossed off.
pages.audio_script: April, May, June. Each month Nia wrote something. Each month the drawer took it. The problem was no longer boring or boasting. The problem was the pile. Any letter she sent now would have to explain the pile, and every explanation she tried sounded worse than silence. I have been busy was a lie. I did not know what to say was true and sounded pathetic. The longer she waited, the bigger the first letter would have to be, and the bigger it had to be, the less she could write it.

vocabulary.definition: So weak or feeble that it makes people feel sorry or embarrassed.
vocabulary.example: My excuse for being late was pathetic.

pages.image_alt: A drawer stuffed with letters, month after month, Nia looking worried.

pages.text: Over the summer Nia's father noticed the drawer would not close. He did not ask what was in it. He asked, instead, whether she wanted to come with him to the post office, where he had a parcel to send. At the counter he weighed the parcel, paid, and then said to the clerk, quite casually, "And how much for a letter to the coast? Say, a thick one. Very thick." The clerk told him. It was the price of an ice cream. Nia said nothing all the way home, and her father did not make her.
pages.illustration_brief: A post office counter: Nia's father sliding a parcel across; Nia beside him looking at a rack of stamps.
pages.audio_script: Over the summer Nia's father noticed the drawer would not close. He did not ask what was in it. He asked, instead, whether she wanted to come with him to the post office, where he had a parcel to send. At the counter he weighed the parcel, paid, and then said to the clerk, quite casually, And how much for a letter to the coast? Say, a thick one. Very thick. The clerk told him. It was the price of an ice cream. Nia said nothing all the way home, and her father did not make her.
pages.image_alt: Nia and her father walking to a red postbox and a post office counter.

pages.text: In September, on the first day of the new school year, Nia sat at her desk and took every letter out of the drawer. Eleven of them, if you counted the one that was just three capital words. She read them in order. The bus stop. The spelling prize. NO, I AM NOT CROSS. A letter about a dog that followed her home in May. A letter about a thunderstorm. One that just said 'I miss you' and then a drawing of the bus. Reading them all at once, she noticed something the drawer had hidden from her: not one of them was boring, and not one of them was boasting. They were just true.
pages.illustration_brief: Eleven letters fanned out across a desk; a small drawing of a bus visible on one.

Eleven of them, if you counted the one that was just three capital words. She read them in order. The bus stop. The spelling prize. NO, I AM NOT CROSS. A letter about a dog that followed her home in May. A letter about a thunderstorm. One that just said I miss you and then a drawing of the bus. Reading them all at once, she noticed something the drawer had hidden from her: not one of them was boring, and not one of them was boasting. They were just true.
pages.image_alt: All the letters spread out over the desk, Nia counting them.

pages.text: She did not write a twelfth letter to explain the eleven. She numbered them instead, one to eleven, in the corner, and put them all in the biggest envelope in the house. On a slip of paper on top she wrote: "These are in order. I wrote one every month. I did not send them because each time I thought it was not good enough, and then because there were too many. I see now that was silly. Start with number one." She did not read it over. She licked the envelope before she could.
pages.illustration_brief: A bulging envelope; Nia's hand writing a number in the corner of a letter; a short note on top.
pages.audio_script: She did not write a twelfth letter to explain the eleven. She numbered them instead, one to eleven, in the corner, and put them all in the biggest envelope in the house. I see now that was silly. Start with number one. She did not read it over. She licked the envelope before she could.
pages.image_alt: Letters each with a small number in the corner going into one large thick envelope.

pages.text: It cost the price of an ice cream, exactly as her father had found out. The clerk weighed it and raised her eyebrows and said nothing. Nia walked home lighter than the envelope, which is not how weight is supposed to work.
pages.illustration_brief: Nia leaving the post office empty-handed, shoulders down and easy; the door swinging behind her.
pages.audio_script: It cost the price of an ice cream, exactly as her father had found out. The clerk weighed it and raised her eyebrows and said nothing. Nia walked home lighter than the envelope, which is not how weight is supposed to work.
pages.image_alt: A post office clerk weighing the fat envelope on a counter scale.

pages.text: Hoa's reply came nine days later. It was thick too. "I read number one on the bus to school and laughed so much a lady moved seats," it began. "I am reading one a day so they last. I am on number six. Bich says hello; she is reading them over my shoulder, which I have told her is rude. Also: I was cross. I am not now. Write to me. Real letters. On paper. But please, Nia, send them."
pages.illustration_brief: Nia on her front step reading a thick letter, laughing; a second girl's doodle in the margin of the letter.
pages.audio_script: Hoa's reply came nine days later. It was thick too. I read number one on the bus to school and laughed so much a lady moved seats, it began. I am reading one a day so they last. I am on number six. Bich says hello; she is reading them over my shoulder, which I have told her is rude. Also: I was cross. I am not now. Write to me. Real letters. On paper. But please, Nia, send them.
pages.image_alt: Nia laughing on the step with Hoa's thick reply, pages spilling out.

pages.text: Nia wrote back that evening. It was one page, about nothing much: the weather, a test, the dog again. She read it over once, decided it was boring, and posted it anyway on the way to school. It arrived. That, she had finally understood, was the only thing a letter really had to do.
pages.illustration_brief: Morning: Nia dropping a thin envelope into a red post box on her way to school, bag on her back, not looking back.

quiz.prompt: Why did Nia not send the first two letters?

options.text: She judged one as boring and the other as boasting
She did not know Hoa's address

quiz.explanation: Page 2: she thought the first was boring and the second sounded like boasting.

quiz.prompt: By June, what was the main thing stopping her?

options.text: The growing pile itself, which any new letter would have to explain

quiz.explanation: Page 4: the problem was no longer boring or boasting. The problem was the pile.

quiz.prompt: What was Nia's father really doing at the post office?

options.text: Quietly showing her that sending a thick letter was easy and cheap
Scolding her in front of the clerk

quiz.explanation: He had noticed the drawer, did not ask, and 'quite casually' asked the price of a very thick letter to the coast (page 5).

quiz.prompt: What did Nia realise when she read all eleven letters together?

options.text: None of them was boring or boasting; they were simply true
They were too long to send

quiz.explanation: Page 6: not one of them was boring, and not one of them was boasting. They were just true.

quiz.prompt: What is the lesson Nia states on the last page?

options.text: A letter's only real job is to arrive
Wait until you have good news

quiz.explanation: Page 10: It arrived. That, she had finally understood, was the only thing a letter really had to do.

quiz.prompt: Hoa wrote 'Are you cross?' in March and 'I was cross' in September. What does the change show?

options.text: In March she hid her feelings behind a question; by September she could say them plainly
Nothing; the two mean the same

quiz.explanation: Page 3's 'Are you cross?' asks about Nia; page 9's 'I was cross. I am not now' admits Hoa's own feeling, once the letters had arrived.

quiz.prompt: Tell a grown-up why Nia's letters stayed in the drawer for a year, what her father and the eleven letters each taught her, and what she did differently at the end.
quiz.rubric: not yet: says she forgot to post them; with support: names one reason with prompting; independent: boring, then boasting, then the pile; father showed sending was easy; reading them together showed they were true; she sent them all numbered and then posted a plain one without judging it
quiz.explanation: The reasons change over the year; a strong retell tracks that change rather than giving one reason.

items.text: Hoa's letter asks: are you cross?
Father asks the price of a thick letter.
Nia reads all eleven letters together.

activities.claim: Nia's father knew about the letters but chose not to ask.

prompts: Have you ever put something off so long that the putting-off became the problem?
Why do you think the father did not simply tell Nia to post the letters?
Nia posted the last letter without reading it twice. Was that careless or wise?

off_screen_prompt: Write a short letter or note to someone today, about nothing special, and give it to them before you can change your mind.
